definition: The principle of rationality (or rationality principle) was coined by Karl R.
details: Popper in his Harvard Lecture of 1963, and published in his book Myth of Framework. It is related to what he called the 'logic of the situation' in an Economica article of 1944/1945, published later in his book The Poverty of Historicism. According to Popper's rationality principle, agents act in the most adequate way according to the objective situation. It is an idealized conception of human behavior which he used to drive his model of situational analysis. Cognitive scientist Allen Newell elaborated on the principle in his account of knowledge level modeling.

explainer.lead: The principle of rationality, coined by Karl Popper in his 1963 Harvard Lecture and published in Myth of Framework, holds that agents act in the most adequate way according to the objective situation. It matters as an idealized model of behavior used to drive situational analysis.

tiers.eli5: Assume people do what makes the most sense given their situation, then explain their actions from that situation.
tiers.practitioner: It is a conceptual tool rather than an algorithm; cognitive scientist Allen Newell elaborated it. A pitfall is treating it as a description of real human behavior, when Popper framed it as an idealized conception.
tiers.paperLevel: According to Popper's rationality principle, agents act in the most adequate way according to the objective situation; it is an idealized conception of human behavior used to drive situational analysis, related to his earlier 'logic of the situation'.

explainer.example: An analyst explains an agent's choice by reconstructing the objective situation and showing the chosen action was the most adequate given it.
